newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF resumes lending to Pakistan, market wary.
newsitem.headline: IMF resumes lending to Pakistan, market wary.

text.p: An IMF move to resume lending to Pakistan, now under a reform-minded caretaker government, failed to boost the stock market on Wednesday, dealers said.

"The market had expected a front-loaded loan but the disbursement is likely to be in small tranches," said dealer Salman Ahmad, as the Karachi 100-share index fell 8.75 points, or 0.63 percent, to 1,387 at midday.
"Most players are cautious as they do not expect foreign investors and local institutions to jump in on the news," dealer Shakeel Anwar said.
On Tuesday the International Monetary Fund approved Pakistan's request to extend a $600 million standby loan to September from March and to increase it by $231 million.
The money will be used to help Pakistan restructure its economy and bring it into better balance.
The decision was a tentative confidence vote in the interim cabinet that took power after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto on disputed corruption charges on November 5.
The IMF had withheld two $80 million tranches of the loan due in June and September because it was unhappy with Pakistan's economic performance and the government's 1996/97 budget plans.
Since then, the country has worked hard to get back into IMF favour with a series of stabilisation and reform measures.

Shahid Javed Burki, finance and economic affairs adviser to the prime minister, told reporters that the IMF would disburse a single $80 million tranche on Thursday, but did not say how future disbursement of remaining IMF funds would be phased.
He said he had initiated discussions on a longer-term loan from the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, which lends to poor countries at just a half percent interest charge.
Burki said no political conditions had been attached to the standby loan at his talks with the IMF in Washington last week.

"The only additional thing is that the Fund is now taking note of the policies, which it calls far-reaching, on the structural front, with emphasis on an improvement in the operations of Pakistan's major banks," he said.

Anisur Rehman, research head at Crosby Securities in Karachi, said the news had ended speculation that the IMF might withhold the loan, but otherwise saw little to cheer the market, saying it had already factored in the expansion of the loan.

"The index will go up, but we do not see a sustainable rally. Lack of liquidity in the market, shortage of funds with local institutions and absence of foreign funds are likely to keep the market from any sharp rise," he said.
"Foreigners are not going to come in until after (February 3) general elections," he said.
The caretaker government plans to rebuild foreign reserves to about $1.5 billion by election time from $788 million now by narrowing the trade deficit and attracting new funds.

Burki had been due to travel to the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday to seek financial help and promote investment in Pakistan's privatisation programme, but said the visit had been postponed to Saturday at the UAE president's request.
Pakistani officials said last month that the UAE had promised a soft loan of up to $500 million, but Burki could not confirm the figure. "We are working on it," he said.

Burki said the IMF had accepted that Pakistan would be unable to achieve its target of limiting domestic bank borrowing to 51 billion rupees ($1.27 billion) at the end of December and had set a new target of 61 billion rupees.
The Bhutto government's June budget for 1996/97 (July-June) set a borrowing target of 30 billion for the whole year, but borrowing had ballooned to 63 billion by the end of October.
Burki said it had gone above 70 billion rupees after the caretaker government's arrival, but was now back at 63 billion.
He said he was sure Pakistan could meet its overall IMF-agreed target of reducing its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product by the end of the financial year.
Bhutto's government said the deficit was five percent of GDP in 1995/96, but it later emerged that the gap was 6.3 percent.
